faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Perryville porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Perryville with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Why do rats keep showing up in the older homes near the Perryville waterfront?
faqs.a: Because the river side of town feeds them and the old foundations house them. Rats travel the waterfront, the rail corridor, and the sewer laterals, and a broken lateral or an open foundation gap gives them a heated base ten feet from the food. Trapping alone cycles forever; the fix is trapping the active animals down while the entries — lateral defects, gnawed sills, open vents — are found and closed. We identify exactly which defects are yours to seal and which belong to a plumber, so the job ends instead of repeating.

faqs.q: A skunk is living under our porch near the river. What happens if you take it out?
faqs.a: Maryland does not allow skunks — a rabies-vector species — to be relocated, so the work is a careful removal followed immediately by screening the porch perimeter with buried wire so the den is physically gone, not just empty. Skunks return to proven dens, and the next skunk in the neighbourhood will test the same hole, so the screen is the part that actually finishes the job. Timing and handling are done to keep the animal calm — a relaxed skunk almost never sprays.

Perryville sits where the Susquehanna meets the Chesapeake, and the river sets its wildlife table. The old river-and-rail town blocks near the waterfront hold raccoons and bats in tall ageing roofs, Norway rats work the waterfront, the rail corridor, and the older commercial foundations, and the marshy edges along the river and Furnace Bay pull skunks and opossums into the yards at the town's edge. Across the river, Havre de Grace gets the postcards; Perryville gets the same river ecology with older housing standing closer to it.

The big campus and corridor change the pattern on the town's other side. Around the VA hospital grounds, the I-95 and Route 40 corridor, and the newer subdivisions toward the Elkton side, the calls turn suburban: squirrels in soffits, groundhogs under sheds and along fence lines, raccoons in chimneys every spring. Perryville's mix means our inspections here run both playbooks — river-town foundations and rat sign down low, suburban roofline work up top — on the same street, sometimes on the same house.
Perryville.extendedBody:
A river town's foundations, a corridor town's roofs

Perryville's oldest homes stand a short walk from the water, on foundations that have been wet-season tested for a century and a half. Rats and skunks use the grade-level failures — crumbled mortar, open crawlspace vents, gaps where additions meet the original house — and raccoons use the roofs above them. We treat the two as one system: seal low and high in the same visit, because a raccoon excluded from the attic will happily test the crawlspace next, and a rat population trapped down without the foundation being closed is back by the next quarter.

Permits and the rules we work under

Our Perryville work is done by a Maryland DNR-licensed Wildlife Damage Control Operator. Maryland does not allow rabies-vector species — raccoons, skunks, foxes — to be relocated, so those jobs are exclusion and sealing work by law as much as by preference. For the river's other regulars, from opossums under porches to groundhogs at the fence line, the approach is the same: remove the animal, then close the structure so the address stops advertising itself.

What we check first in Perryville

The foundation and crawlspace vents at grade, the sewer cleanouts and shared walls where rats travel, the chimney cap situation, and every roof junction where an addition changed the pitch. Waterfront-adjacent homes get an extra look at bulkhead-side burrows and the outbuildings near the shore, where skunks and groundhogs split their time between the marsh edge and your yard.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Rising Sun?
faqs.a: They do in Cecil County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

faqs.q: Groundhogs are digging under our bank barn. How serious is that?
faqs.a: Serious enough to act on this season. A groundhog system under a barn bank or slab removes the soil the structure stands on, run by run, and the repair bill for a undermined barn dwarfs the removal bill every time. We take out the resident groundhogs, collapse and backfill the burrow runs so the system cannot simply be re-claimed, and screen the vulnerable edges. If the floor has already cracked or a wall has started to move, we will show you the burrow map so your builder sees the full extent.

faqs.q: The raccoons split their time between our barn and our house chimney. Can you solve both?
faqs.a: That is the normal pattern here, and yes — it has to be solved as one job. Sealing the chimney while the barn loft stays open just gives you a raccoon with a shorter commute. We work the property as a system: the den in the house is excluded and the flue capped, the barn harbourage is cleared and its entries closed, and the route between them is broken. One visit planned as a property job costs less than three separate call-outs chasing the same animals.

Rising Sun is farm country first, and its wildlife calls come off the land. This is Cecil County's horse-and-dairy heart, a few fields from the Mason-Dixon line, and the pattern here is groundhogs in the pasture fence lines and under bank barns, raccoons in barn lofts and then in the farmhouse chimney, skunks under every porch and outbuilding with a dirt floor, and bats in the tall attics of the old farmhouses along the Octoraro. A Rising Sun call usually involves more than the house — the animals run a route between the barn, the woodlot, and the roof, and sealing one stop just reroutes them to the next.

The town itself adds the village version of the same list. Rising Sun's older in-town homes, built when the crossroads served the farms around it, get squirrels at the soffit line and raccoons in chimneys each spring, and the newer subdivisions spreading from the town edge put fresh housing directly against old pasture — groundhog burrows in the back fence within a season, every time. Our inspections here are property inspections: house, barn, sheds, and the fence lines between, read as one system.
Rising Sun.extendedBody:
Barns, fence lines, and farmhouse roofs: one animal route

On a Cecil County farm property, the raccoon in the chimney probably spent the fall in the barn loft, and the groundhog under the shed has cousins in the pasture fence. Farm work here starts with the route, not the building: which structures are feeding and housing the animals, in what order, and what has to be closed so the route breaks. Bank barns deserve their own warning — a groundhog system under a barn bank or a slab edge undermines quietly for years, and the first sign is often a cracked floor or a listing wall. Catching that early is the cheapest version of the job by a wide margin.

How the work is permitted in Maryland

Every Rising Sun job is handled by a Maryland DNR-licensed Wildlife Damage Control Operator. Maryland law does not allow rabies-vector species — raccoons, skunks, and foxes — to be relocated, so those animals are dealt with by exclusion and sealing, and the sealing is specified for farm life: buried wire on porch and shed perimeters, caps on farmhouse flues, and hardware cloth that survives weather and livestock. A fix that lasts one season on a farm is not a fix.

Rising Sun's other regulars

Opossums under porches and in outbuildings, squirrels in the in-town soffits, and bats in the farmhouse attics along the creek bottoms round out the list. Octoraro Creek and its branches thread the whole area, and the animals follow the water and the woodlots it connects — which is why a property's tree line and creek edge are part of every inspection we do here, not scenery.
